Chapter 7. Lessons in Leadership—Redefining Strength and Service.
You know, leadership isn’t really about always having the right answer—or pretending you never make mistakes. It’s about showing up, even when it’s tough. After the election, a lot of people started to see leadership in a new light. It stopped being just about titles, and started being about action—about listening, learning, and lifting each other up.
Picture this: a community organizer, completely worn out but still determined, gathers a group of neighbors in a church basement. The air’s thick with honesty. People talk openly about their fears, their anger, and their hopes for what comes next. Nobody in that room has all the answers. But the simple act of coming together, of sharing and listening—that takes real courage.
For some, leadership actually meant stepping back a little, making space for new voices to be heard. It meant mentoring young activists, passing on hard-earned lessons, and cheering others on as they take their own risks. The old, top-down model of leadership—the kind that’s rigid and authoritative—started to fade. In its place, something much more collaborative and compassionate began to grow.
And here’s something to really pay attention to: Real strength isn’t about never showing weakness. It’s about being honest with yourself, admitting when you’re wrong, and reaching out when you need help. A lot of us fall into the trap of thinking we have to do everything alone. But progress? It’s always a team effort.
That campaign experience—with all its ups and downs—became a well of wisdom. It taught everyone that leadership is a journey, not a finish line. It’s about showing up, again and again, even when the road ahead is unclear. And above all, it’s about believing that together, we really can build something better.
